props.title: The Sun Also Rises

sections.content: Ernest Hemingway's celebrated novel gets lavish CinemaScope treatment in The Sun Also Rises (1957), with Tyrone Power and Ava Gardner embodying the Lost Generation's restless spirit. Director Henry King captures the sun-drenched beauty of post-WWI Paris and Pamplona, though some of Hemingway's raw emotional edge gets smoothed into Hollywood glamour. The film belongs to a vital 1950s wave of Hemingway adaptations including The Old Man and the Sea (1958) and A Farewell to Arms (1957), as studios sought prestige properties that could showcase both literary credentials and exotic European locations.

sections.content: The film's greatest strength lies in its atmospheric recreation of 1920s expatriate life. While The Sun Also Rises sanitizes some of Hemingway's themes of impotence and alcoholism, it excels in capturing the endless rounds of drinks, parties and bullfights that defined the era's restless search for meaning. Mel Ferrer's portrayal of injured war veteran Jake Barnes lacks some of the novel's bitter edge, but Ava Gardner brings authentic world-weary sensuality to Brett Ashley. The Pamplona sequences, featuring actual footage from the Running of the Bulls, provide visceral authenticity.

The production marked a fascinating transition point in Hollywood's treatment of "serious" literature. While earlier Hemingway adaptations like For Whom the Bell Tolls (1943) emphasized romantic spectacle, The Sun Also Rises attempts to engage more directly with themes of post-war disillusionment and moral drift. This approach would influence later literary adaptations like The Great Gatsby (1974) in balancing period glamour with social commentary. SUBHEAD: Lost Generation on Film

sections.content: The film fits into a larger cinematic exploration of the Lost Generation, from Midnight in Paris (2011) to The Great Gatsby (2013). While modern films can more explicitly deal with the era's sexual politics and psychological trauma, The Sun Also Rises deserves credit for bringing Hemingway's portrait of expatriate ennui to mainstream audiences, even in somewhat sanitized form. The film's gorgeous location photography and strong ensemble cast create an intoxicating portrait of a generation searching for meaning amid the cafes and bullrings of Europe.
